context.in_practice: Only one case differs between routes: running with no directory given. Route 1 prints the full path of the current folder; routes 2 and 3 print `.`. If you pass a directory, every route prints it exactly as typed, so a symlink shows its own name rather than its target. The other differences belong to single arms and not to the route chosen: an arm on route 1 that accepts `--theatre` before the command, the varied Ctrl-C exit codes on route 1, and the traceback on route 2.
context.stakes: When `config watch` starts, its first line tells you which directory it is watching. If you didn't pass a directory, that line either names the real folder or just says `.`, which only helps if you already know where you launched it. A directory you pass yourself is printed exactly as you typed it on every route, so that line never reveals where a symlink actually points.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 tells you where it's watching when you didn't say, but prints the cwd path unresolved, so on macOS it may show /var where the real path is /private/var. Routes 2 and 3 print a bare `.`, which is simple but tells you nothing about the location.

plan_why: Starts `config watch` four times and captures the `watching <dir>` line each prints. The four starts are: no --theatre (route 1 should print the absolute cwd, route 2 '.'), `--theatre .` placed before `config`, `--theatre=sub`, and `--theatre linked` (a symlink to sub), which shows whether the path is printed as given or resolved. A hand edit made during the first watch, followed by `history`, checks that the watch really picked up changes.
routes: --theatre or TROUPE_THEATRE as given; the absolute cwd when neither is set
